title: I spent three months full time building a game. 476 commits later, the hardest part wasn't writing code.
author: happypird
selftext:
# 

I've been building **Genius Simulator** solo for about three months. 476 commits so far.

AI wrote part of the code. But deciding what to build, what to cut, and what to tell the AI to stop doing? That's where most of the actual work went.

The game is build around one joke: "genius" who does almost nothing. You sip tea, glance to the right, or make some other completely ordinary gesture. The experts around you interpret it as a profound strategic move, turn it into a world-changing invention, and somehow use it to stop the apocalypse.

The apocalypse is real. The genius is questionable. The experts are absolutely certain they've understood everything. And Even players see thought the genius's... logic ?

**Genius Simulator, Tea, Sip, Apocalypse.**

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5142470/Genius\_Simulator](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5142470/Genius_Simulator)

I originally wanted to share the game, but I figured the development workflow might be more useful to this sub. Here's what actually worked, what failed, and what I ended up doing differently.

# 1. I had to teach AI how to play my game

At first, I'd ask Claude to playtest. It would take a screenshot, think about it, click something, take another screenshot, and repeat.

Meanwhile, the game runs at 60 FPS. Claude's reaction time is measured in seconds. Even dragging a menu was a struggle, and the screenshots ate through tokens.

Eventually, I added a `debug` mode that exposes the battle state and development handles for the game's systems. The agent can now inject a small control loop directly into the running page and let the game play itself at full speed. It reads the results afterwards.

Screenshots are now mainly for showing me what happened, not for making the agent understand every frame.

I even have a bot that can solve the tilt-maze minigame.

This was probably one of the most useful changes I made. Instead of making the AI better at clicking, I changed the way it interacts with the game.

# 2. AI-generated pixel art isn't necessarily pixel art

This one cost me more time than I expected.

Image models can produce something that looks pixelated at a glance, but the pixels don't actually follow a consistent grid. Different parts have different pixel sizes, and the shapes drift between animation frames.

My first solution was to automate the cleanup: quantize the colors, sample each cell, and pick the most common color.

It deformed the sprites. Animation frames flickered.

The solution was less clever: measure the shapes by eye, work on a proper low-resolution grid, and reuse the same base image across animation frames.

My current rule is simple. If an automated fix gets the result wrong, I stop trying to automate that particular problem and do it manually.

AI saves time, but sometimes the time you save generating an asset gets spent fixing it afterwards.

# 3. Rebuilding something in 3D doesn't mean it gets better

I had a tilt-maze scene that I'd already tuned by hand in 2D.

Then AI rebuilt the whole thing in WebGL.

It looked worse and ran slower.

I reverted the entire thing and kept only the 3D ball.

That was a useful reminder that switching to newer technology doesn't automatically improve a finished piece of work. Sometimes the correct solution is to keep the part that already works.

# 4. I had to write rules before letting AI write comedy

The game's central joke is that people interpret ordinary actions as evidence of extraordinary genius.

Left to its own devices, AI tends to explain the joke, add unnecessary context, and turn a short popup into a paragraph.

So I wrote a one-page writing guide myself and made the AI follow it.

One rule made a noticeable difference: **a single text popup must fit within three lines or ten seconds.**

If the player needs to stop playing for too long just to understand a joke, something has gone wrong.

Localization has the same problem. Translating a joke literally often kills it. For twelve languages, I decide the appropriate voice and register first, then rewrite the joke for that language.

It's localization, not translation.

# 5. Asking AI to review AI was mostly a waste of tokens

I tried using sub-agents to compare different versions blindly and choose the better one.

It consumed tokens without producing meaningful improvements.

What worked better was writing a short, concrete checklist myself and asking the agent to check against it.

Things like:

* Does the trailer open with actual gameplay?
* Is any shot reused?
* Does the scene communicate what it's supposed to communicate?

I also learned not to let AI casually adjust my game balance. It kept "improving" numbers that I'd already decided on.

Now the rule is that numbers in the specification are requirements, not suggestions.

# 6. The trailer needed fewer shots, not more

I generated concept-art animations with edit tool and used an FFmpeg script to assemble the trailer. Every cut is defined in an edit list and aligned to the music's bars.

The first AI-generated edit had 73 shots in 50 seconds, practically one cut per beat.

It was flickering garbage with no coherent progression.

I cut the number of shots roughly in half and built the trailer around one idea:

**The genius does something tiny → the world interprets it as a master plan.**



That gave the trailer an actual throughline instead of just a sequence of things happening quickly.

# What I've learned so far

AI made it possible for me to build this game at a speed I probably couldn't have managed alone.

But the difficult decisions didn't disappear. They moved somewhere else.

I spent less time typing code and more time figuring out:

* How to give AI reliable access to the game's internal state.
* Which tasks are worth automating and which aren't.
* What rules the AI needs to follow to produce usable results.
* When to reject an output instead of trying to salvage it.

I'm still working on the game, so this isn't a claim that I've figured everything out. These are just the things that made a real difference to my workflow.

If you're also building a game with AI, I'm interested in hearing what has and hasn't worked for you.

And if you want to see what all this effort actually produced, the demo is here(don't forget to wishlist it):

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5142470/Genius\_Simulator](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5142470/Genius_Simulator)
